domain: Transportation Policy / Coordination Systems / Path Dependence
topic_summary: Analysis of the traffic convention mandating which side of the road vehicles drive on (right-hand vs left-hand). This is a coordination equilibrium with high switching costs, not a contested kernel—all parties agree on what the constraint is (a single coordination rule) and disagree only on which equilibrium to select or whether switching is worth the cost.

key_entities: National traffic authority (enforcement body setting the rule)
Vehicle operators (drivers, cyclists, pedestrians adapting to the rule)
Infrastructure (roads, signage, vehicle design standardized to the rule)
key_tensions: Coordination benefit of uniformity vs switching cost of changing equilibrium

axes.human_readable: Coordination Equilibrium Lock-In (Network Effects of Handedness Choice)
axes.structural_delta: Once a handedness convention is adopted, network effects (vehicle design, infrastructure, driver training, cross-border compatibility) create self-reinforcing lock-in
axes.primary_observable: Switching cost estimates (infrastructure redesign, vehicle fleet replacement, accident rates during transition); number of countries sharing each convention
axes.selection_reason: Upstream mountain providing physical/coordination constraint base

axes.human_readable: Switching Cost Barrier (Path Dependence Preventing Convergence)
axes.structural_delta: The cost of switching from one equilibrium to the other (infrastructure, fleet, retraining) prevents convergence to a single global standard despite efficiency gains
axes.primary_observable: Historical switching attempts (Sweden 1967, Samoa 2009); cost-benefit analyses of proposed switches; accident rate data during transitions
axes.selection_reason: Downstream rope documenting the coordination trap; structurally distinct from mountain

axes.structural_delta: Current global distribution of left-hand vs right-hand driving reflects colonial-era power projection and post-independence path dependence
axes.primary_observable: Correlation between former colonial power and current traffic handedness; post-independence switching decisions
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: historical explanation for current distribution but does not add independent structural constraint beyond coordination_equilibrium_lock_in

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Current distribution reflects colonial-era diffusion and post-independence path dependence
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Historical explanation for distribution pattern; does not add independent constraint structure beyond coordination_equilibrium_lock_in mountain

omegas.description: Topic was flagged as candidate contested kernel but is NOT a genuine kernel. All parties agree on what the constraint is (a coordination rule mandating one side of the road). Disagreement is about WHICH equilibrium to select (right vs left) or whether switching cost is worth paying—not about what kind of constraint exists. This is observer-position disagreement about a single constraint, not multiple readings of a shared commitment that emit different constraints. No readings to decompose.

Is there a measurable safety difference between right-hand and left-hand driving (e.g., due to dominant eye or hand)? If yes, the mountain may have a weak directional preference; if no, pure coordination game.
Do autonomous vehicles reduce switching costs (software update vs driver retraining) enough to enable future convergence? If yes, the rope may weaken; if no, lock-in persists.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Topic is a straightforward coordination equilibrium with path dependence, not a contested kernel.
